s: Part two.
Coordinators and subagents.
This is task statement one point two: orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns.
By the end of this part, you'll know how to pick between one agent, a coordinator, and plain code.
Why everything routes through the hub.
When to fan out.
And how to bound the whole tree.
Let's start with a picture.
You send three people into a supermarket, each with a third of the list.
You stand at the entrance.
You hold the list.
You decide who takes what.
And you check the trolley at the end.
They walk the aisles.
What do you gain?
You never hear about the aisles.
Three people walked for an hour, and you got three short reports.
What do you pay?
None of them can see the others' baskets.
And you pay for all three trips, whether or not you use what they bring.
That's a coordinator.
And there's a third option people skip.
If you know exactly what's on the list, in what order, and it's the same every week, you don't need anyone exercising judgment at all.
You need a checklist, and someone following it.
The technical names are these.
Three shapes.
One.
A single agent, running one loop.
Two.
A coordinator with subagents.
Three.
A deterministic pipeline.
That means plain code that runs fixed steps in a fixed order.
When does each one fit, and how does each one fail?
A single agent suits one thread of reasoning, where each step depends on the last.
It fails by filling its context window, and losing early instructions.
A coordinator with subagents suits independent subtasks that each produce a lot of verbose intermediate work.
Each subagent keeps that work in its own window.
Only its final message returns.
It fails through fan-out cost, duplicated work, and context lost at the boundary.
A deterministic pipeline suits work whose steps and order are known in advance.
It's predictable.
It's easy to cost.
And it fails only by meeting something its author did not anticipate.
The deciding test is one question.
Does the next step depend on the content of the previous result?
Compile, then test, then deploy.
That's a pipeline.
Read a failure, form a hypothesis, choose where to look next.
That's an agent.
And very often, the best answer is a narrow agent inside one stage of a pipeline.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
An on-call assistant reads an arbitrary production alert.
It picks each next diagnostic, out of about forty, based on what the last one returned.
A platform lead wants to replace it with a fixed pipeline that runs a standard set, in a standard order.
The surrounding steps never vary: opening a ticket, attaching output, and paging the owner.
What's the right design?
Take a second.
Think of a hospital.
It doesn't let doctors improvise the admission paperwork.
And it doesn't force them to follow a fixed script when diagnosing.
The forms follow a checklist.
The diagnosis follows the clues.
The answer.
Make the fixed steps a deterministic pipeline.
Keep a bounded agent loop only for the diagnosis stage.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: replace everything with the fixed pipeline.
Why?
A fixed order can't follow an alert where each result decides the next step.
So it runs irrelevant checks, and misses the right one.
Wrong: run all forty diagnostics as parallel subagents.
Why?
That pays for every branch, whether needed or not.
And it ignores the dependency between steps.
Wrong: keep one agent for the whole workflow, with a higher turn cap.
Why?
That pays latency and unpredictability to rediscover a flowchart you already own.
And it risks a skipped page.
Question two.
The notes run the same idea the other way round.
Here's the scenario.
A release-notes generator fetches a diff, classifies the change, renders a paragraph, and appends it.
Always in that order.
A colleague proposes a coordinator with four specialist subagents.
What's the answer?
Take a second.
The answer.
A deterministic pipeline in code, with a single narrow model call for classification.
Why?
Because classification is the only step that needs judgment.
Hold on to this line.
If you can draw the flowchart before the run, write code.
Use an agent only where the next step depends on what you just learned.
Next, the rule that workers don't talk to each other.
In plain words, everything goes through the coordinator.
That's slower on paper, and safer in practice.
Pilots talk to the control tower, not to each other.
Two pilots chatting directly might be quicker.
But then nobody holds the full picture.
And there's no record of who was told what.
The technical name is the hub-and-spoke pattern.
Subagents never communicate directly.
All routing passes through the coordinator.
That gives you two things.
First, observability, meaning one complete record of every handoff.
Second, central error handling, meaning one place where failures are detected and routed.
The coordinator owns the plan, the budget, and the acceptance criteria.
The subagents own the work.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A research coordinator routes each search subagent's findings to a report writer.
An engineer proposes letting the search subagents send findings straight to the writer, to save latency.
Compliance requires a complete record of what each worker received and produced.
And one place where failures are handled.
What do you do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Keep all communication routed through the coordinator.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: approve direct routing, and have each subagent log its own messages.
Why?
That rebuilds the record after the fact.
And it removes the single point where failures are caught.
Wrong: allow direct routing only for high-confidence findings.
Why?
A partial bypass still breaks the record, for exactly the traffic that skips the hub.
Wrong: merge search and writing into one subagent.
Why?
That floods the writer's window with verbose search output.
And it still doesn't meet the audit requirement.
The constraint words are "complete record" and "one place where failures are handled."
Those make the hub non-negotiable.
Now a failure that looks like a quality problem, and is really a structure problem.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A market research coordinator spawns four parallel subagents.
One.
Analyst reports.
Two.
Regulatory filings.
Three.
Earnings call transcripts.
Four.
Social sentiment.
Each returns a solid, well-cited summary.
Runs are fast.
But clients complain the final report never connects a regulatory change to the sentiment shift that followed.
What's missing?
Take a second.
Four reporters each cover one beat for a newspaper, and every story is excellent.
But no editor reads all four.
So nobody notices that the council vote in one story explains the protest in another.
The fix is an editor, not bigger notebooks.
The answer.
In exam terms, the four lanes really are independent, so the parallel fan-out is correct.
What's missing is a stage responsible for cross-source synthesis.
Siloed output from a multi-agent system usually signals a missing aggregation step.
Not a model problem.
Not a context problem.
So you add an explicit synthesis step.
Such as a cross-source subagent whose job is finding intersections.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a bigger context window for each subagent.
Why?
Nothing in the design asks anyone to connect the lanes, however much they can hold.
Wrong: let the four subagents exchange findings directly.
Why?
That breaks hub and spoke.
Wrong: give every subagent all four source tools.
Why?
That undoes the decomposition.
It roughly quadruples cost.
And it still leaves nobody owning synthesis.
Hold on to this line.
Siloed results mean nobody was given the job of joining them up.
Next, speed.
In plain words, if three jobs don't need each other's answers, start them all at once.
The total wait becomes the slowest job, not the sum of all three.
You need quotes from three builders.
Calling the first, waiting a week, then calling the second, triples the wait for nothing.
No quote depends on another.
So you ask all three on the same day.
The technical version.
Each delegation is a tool call.
A coordinator that issues one delegation call per turn, waits, then issues the next, runs its subagents in sequence.
A coordinator that emits several delegation calls in a single response runs them in parallel.
Latency then equals the slowest branch.
Question five.
Here's the scenario.
A code modernisation coordinator analyses three independent modules, about four minutes each.
The phase takes twelve minutes.
The transcripts show one call, a wait, then the next.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Emit all three subagent calls in a single response.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: switch to a smaller model.
Why?
It may trim each branch, but it keeps the serial structure.
Wrong: raise the concurrent-subagent limit.
Why?
The documented default is twenty.
That's far more than three.
So that isn't what serialises them.
Wrong: merge the three into one subagent.
Why?
It's still sequential.
And it pulls all three modules into one window.
The signature to recognise: latency roughly three times what it should be.
Now the contrast, because the exam tests it from both sides.
The deciding test for parallel versus sequential is this.
Does any branch need another branch's findings?
Findings.
Not files.
Three auditors reading three different service directories are independent.
An auditor and a remediation planner are sequential.
Even if they open no common file.
Why?
Because the planner's input is the auditor's output.
Question six.
The notes include one on exactly this.
Here's the scenario.
A coordinator spawns three vendor research subagents.
And at the same time, a fourth that writes the recommendation.
The recommendation keeps citing things the summaries contradict.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Run the recommender after the other three.
Parallel fan-out over dependent stages gives you full cost, plus branches that contradict each other.
There's a failure-handling difference too.
A sequential chain stops, and reports the stage that failed.
A parallel fan-out collects each branch's outcome.
So one failed branch doesn't void the others.
Hold on to this line.
Parallel when no branch needs another's findings.
Sequential when it does.
And the test runs through conclusions, not the filesystem.
Question seven.
One more coordinator failure from the notes.
Here's the scenario.
A team adds subagents to a data quality agent, expecting token use to fall.
Instead, it rises by about eighty percent.
And the main conversation still fills up, even though the subagents return concise summaries.
What's the cause?
Take a second.
The answer.
The coordinator is re-reading the same tables, and rerunning the same queries, after its workers report.
It pays for the work twice.
The fix is to constrain the coordinator's own tools.
And instruct it to gather, combine and route.
Not to investigate.
Now the wrong turn.
Wrong: each subagent inherits the parent's full history.
It's tempting.
Why is it wrong?
Because it doesn't.
A subagent starts fresh.
Now bounding the tree.
In plain words, anything that can delegate can delegate to something that delegates.
Left alone, one request can grow into a tree of agents.
And the bill grows with it.
So you need two things.
One limit on money that covers everyone.
And one rule on how many layers of delegation are allowed.
Picture a project manager.
They give the team one company card, whose limit covers everyone.
And they rule that contractors may not hire subcontractors.
Limiting how many phone calls each contractor makes wouldn't stop one expensive purchase.
And a polite request not to subcontract is easy to ignore.
The technical version has four settings.
I'll take them one at a time.
First.
The coordinator delegates through a built-in tool called Agent.
That tool must be listed in the coordinator's allowedTools.
If it isn't, every delegation falls through to a permission decision.
And in modes that never prompt, it's denied.
The symptom?
Claude doing all the work itself, with no Agent calls anywhere in the transcript.
Second. maxBudgetUsd covers the whole tree.
Why?
Because subagent requests count toward the query's total_cost_usd.
At the cap, the query refuses new subagents.
Third.
The environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH caps nesting.
It defaults to three layers below the main agent.
Setting it to one lets the main agent delegate, while its workers cannot.
Fourth.
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS caps how many run at once.
It defaults to twenty.
Beyond that, a spawn fails with the message "Concurrent subagent limit reached."
And the notes add one thing.
Opus-class models delegate more readily than earlier ones.
So these bounds matter more than they used to.
Question eight.
This one is pick two.
Here's the scenario.
A research coordinator on an Opus-class model grew a tree three layers deep.
It cost several times its estimate.
The architect must bound total spend, including subagents.
And stop workers spawning workers.
While the coordinator keeps delegating.
Which two?
Take a second.
The answers.
First.
Set maxBudgetUsd on the coordinator's query.
Second.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to one.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: set maxTurns on each subagent.
Why?
That bounds round trips, not dollars.
And one turn reading a huge file can cost more than many cheap turns.
Wrong: remove Agent from the coordinator's allowedTools.
Why?
That stops the coordinator delegating, which the requirements forbid.
Wrong: add a prompt sentence saying subagents must never create subagents.
Why?
Nothing enforces it.
And the coordinator's prompt doesn't even cross into the subagents.
Question nine.
A contrast worth holding.
What if only one specific subagent must never delegate, while others still can?
Here's the scenario, from the notes.
A reviewer that someone gave the Agent tool.
It produced a tree four layers deep.
What's the narrowest fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Remove Agent from that one subagent's tools list.
Or add it to its disallowedTools.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: set spawn depth to one.
Why?
That would stop every subagent delegating.
It over-applies the fix.
Wrong: the budget cap.
Why?
It only cuts the tree off partway, after money is spent.
Wrong: the concurrency cap.
Why?
It limits width, not depth.
So here's the contrast.
Depth and budget bound the whole tree.
Removing the tool from one agent makes that agent structurally unable.
Last in this part: what a budget stop means.
Question ten.
Here's the scenario.
A due-diligence coordinator runs three researcher subagents under a max_budget_usd cap.
On a run that hits the cap, it publishes a report from the two researchers that finished, and labels it complete.
The third was stopped mid-work.
Analysts act on the report, without knowing a third of the sources were never covered.
What should happen?
Take a second.
A survey team runs out of money after two of three towns.
It publishes "the region's results".
Readers assume all three towns were counted.
The honest report says two of three towns were surveyed, and the third was not reached.
The answer.
In exam terms, at the cap the query stops background subagents, and ends with the subtype error_max_budget_usd.
That's an incomplete result, not a partial success.
The wrapper must check the subtype before trusting the result.
And carry the coverage gap into the human-facing output.
Two of three sources, with the third named.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the cap.
Why?
The failure becomes rarer.
And the next capped run is mislabelled the same way.
Wrong: remove the cap, and rely on maxTurns.
Why?
Runaway cost risk.
And turns don't bound money.
Wrong: tell the coordinator in its prompt to mention missing sources.
Why?
That's advisory.
And the coordinator may not even know which worker was stopped.
The reliable signal is the subtype.
We'll meet coverage reporting again in the chapter on context management and reliability.
There, the rule is this.
Eleven of thirteen is reported as eleven of thirteen, with the two named.
That's part two.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Pick the shape by asking whether the next step depends on the last result.
Route everything through the hub.
Fan out only what is independent.
Cap the whole tree's money and depth.
And never call a capped run complete.
Coming up in part three: spawning subagents and passing context.
